definition.text: A regressive change in which a stable soil loses its equilibrium; more broadly, any disturbance to a soil judged harmful or undesirable.

facts.text: Degradation, also called pedolysis, departs from natural soil evolution: climax vegetation is replaced by secondary plant communities, which changes the amount and makeup of humus.
Degradation is directly tied to human activity, whereas its companion process, retrogression, is driven mainly by soil erosion.
Soil erosion is the main factor in soil degradation, acting through water erosion, wind erosion, chemical degradation and physical degradation.
Roads add impermeable surfaces that cause runoff and soil loss; overgrazing, monoculture, row cropping, tillage, crop removal and land-use conversion speed up erosion.
Soils naturally reach high productivity and then decline as mineral nutrients are removed, so older soils are more vulnerable to induced degradation.
Globally, the quality of 33% of pastureland, 25% of arable land and 23% of forests has deteriorated over the last 30 years; 3.2 billion people depend on this land.
Erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination remain serious concerns for agricultural soils.

title: Soil retrogression
article: Soil retrogression and degradation#Perturbations of the balance of a soil

definition.text: The reversion of a soil toward pioneer conditions, mainly through erosion of its upper horizons after its vegetation is destroyed.

facts.text: A soil at its climax tends to stay stable: vegetation supplies humus, moves material upward and shields the ground from water and wind, while roots bind its particles.
After a disturbance, secondary succession usually takes over, and it runs much faster than primary succession because a soil already exists.
When vegetation is destroyed on a large scale, by an avalanche or by people, erosion strips the upper horizons; retrogression can be partial or total, leaving bare rock.
Clearing a sloping site exposed to violent rains can destroy its soil completely.

Clearing, excessive cutting, forest grazing and litter raking replace climax vegetation, as when broadleaf forest gives way to moorland or pine plantations; retrogression often stems from very old practices.
Cycles of succession and regression follow each other over short intervals under human action or over long intervals under climatic change.

definition.text: The steady balance that a soil and its vegetation reach after evolving together, the highest development its environment can produce.

facts.text: Bare rock is colonized first by lichens and mosses, then by herbs, shrubs and forest, while a humus-bearing A horizon and then mineral B horizons form.
Some ecologists call the balanced stage the climax, others the natural potential; succession is the evolution toward it.
Soil evolution cycles last from tens to thousands of years for quickly evolving soils with only an A horizon to more than a million years for slowly developing ones.
The regional climate and its biome set the general course, while parent rock and local drainage explain specialized associations such as peat bogs.

title: Soil enhancement and rebuilding
article: Soil retrogression and degradation#Soil enhancement, rebuilding, and regeneration

definition.text: Practices that counter erosion and rebuild a degraded soil, chiefly by improving its structure, adding organic matter and limiting runoff.

facts.text: Such techniques can never fully restore a soil, with its fauna and flora, that took more than a thousand years to build.
On low-clay soils in northern Thailand, one application of 200 kg of bentonite per rai (6.26 rai = 1 hectare) helped retain water and nutrients and raised yields by an average of 73%.
A 2008 survey of 250 farmers in northeast Thailand found output 18% higher among clay users, and some had switched to vegetables, which need more fertile soil.
Bentonite applied to degraded sandy soils also reduced the risk of crop failure in drought years.

definition.text: A process in which land becomes less healthy and productive through human activities or natural conditions.

facts.text: The 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment defined it as the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of drylands.
The FAO describes it as a persistent decline in land's ability to sustain ecosystem functions and services, driven by deforestation, overgrazing and unsustainable farming.
Human activities, above all unsustainable land management, are usually the main cause; natural hazards are excluded, though people can indirectly affect floods and wildfires.
It reduces agricultural productivity, causes biodiversity loss and can reduce food security and water security.
It can weaken the land's natural capacity to store and filter water, leading to water scarcity.
Its impacts range from subtle productivity losses to the complete abandonment of farmland.
What one group sees as degradation another may see as an opportunity: a steep, rainy slope worries scientists about erosion but may promise farmers high yields.
In 2007 up to 40% of the world's agricultural land was estimated to be seriously degraded, and the UN estimated the global economy could lose $23 trillion by 2050.

title: Global extent of land degradation

definition.text: How much of the world's land is degraded and how many people live on it, as estimated by the UN, the IPCC and others.

facts.text: The IPCC's 2019 Special Report on Climate Change and Land put about a quarter of Earth's ice-free land under human-induced degradation (medium confidence).
Erosion from farm fields runs 11 to 20 times (no-tillage) to more than 100 times (conventional tillage) faster than soil forms.
In 2014 the UN estimated that around 30% of land was degraded, with around 3.2 billion people living in the degrading areas.
About 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded every year, through exploitation without planning for long-term sustainability.
In 2024 the UN claimed that 75% of soils are degraded to some extent; the share might rise to 90% by 2050 if current trends continue.
In 2025 around 1.7 billion people lived where degradation causes sizeable crop yield losses, nearly 1 billion of them in middle-income countries.
Eastern and Southern Asia hold the largest affected populations, combining a large accumulated degradation debt with high population densities.
In 2021 two-thirds of Africa's productive land was claimed to be severely affected by land degradation.

conflicts.text: About 1 million km2 of soil was degraded every year in 2015–2019.
conflicts.note: Roughly eight times the 120,000 km2 of productive land a year given in S:d3910d94f492; the two may count different land, so verify.

notes: The share-of-land figures (quarter of ice-free land, IPCC 2019; 30%, UN 2014; 75% of soils to some extent, UN 2024; up to 40% of agricultural land, 2007, S:cad4120fad63) differ by date and by what is counted, so they are stated as separate facts, not conflicts.

definition.text: The forms land degradation takes, from long-known erosion and physical, chemical and biological decline to newer forms such as pollution and land loss.

facts.text: Types known for centuries are water, wind and mechanical erosion and physical, chemical and biological degradation.
Four types have emerged in the last 50 years: pollution, loss of arable land to construction and expansion, artificial radioactivity, and land-use limits from armed conflict.
More than 36 types can be assessed, all caused or worsened by people, among them erosion, contamination, acidification, sheet erosion, silting, aridification, salinization and urbanization.

definition.text: The many interrelated human and natural drivers of land degradation, both proximate and underlying.

facts.text: Proximate drivers are biophysical factors and unsustainable land management; underlying drivers are social, economic and institutional.
Land degradation is largely tied to agriculture, deforestation and climate change; clearcutting and overlogging are among the land-clearance causes.
More than 1 660 Mha, over 10 percent of the world's land area, has been degraded by unsustainable land use and management, more than 60% of it on cropland and pasture.
Leaving soil bare after harvest and deep plowing deplete nutrients; areas under conventional tillage degrade 5-10 times faster than no-till areas.
Monocultures, overgrazing beyond the livestock carrying capacity and inappropriate irrigation also degrade land.
Soil pollution from littering, urbanization, mining, oil spills, pesticides, herbicides, fertilizers and animal waste adds to the damage.
High population density is not always linked to degradation; it is people's practices that degrade a landscape.

title: Climate change and land degradation
article: Land degradation#Climate change and land degradation

definition.text: The worsening of land degradation by climate change, especially in low-lying coasts, river deltas, drylands and permafrost areas.

facts.text: From 1961 to 2013 the area of drylands in drought grew by more than 1% a year.
In 2015 about 500,000,000 people lived in areas that had undergone desertification during the 1980s–2000s, and they are severely affected by climate change.
Some 74% of the world's poor are reported to be directly affected by land degradation.
Sea-level rise can flood river deltas and low islands with seawater, raising salinity until farming becomes impossible in very low-lying areas.
The 2022 IPCC report found degradation responding more directly to climate change, with all types of erosion and soil organic matter decline increasing.
Degraded land also releases greenhouse gases, which worsens climate change.
Heavy rainfall and extreme weather make erosion, soil degradation and compaction more likely.

related: Effects of climate change on agriculture

title: Impacts of land degradation

definition.text: The harm degraded land and soil cause: lost productivity, food insecurity, water pollution, biodiversity loss, natural hazards and economic costs.

facts.text: Results include lower crop yields, less diverse ecosystems, more vulnerability to floods and droughts, people losing their homes, less food and economic problems.
Productive capacity declines temporarily or permanently, seen as lost biomass, lost actual or potential productivity, or changed vegetation cover and soil nutrients.
Slight degradation cuts yield potential by 10% and moderate degradation by 10–50%; severely degraded soils have lost more than 50% of their potential.
Most severely degraded soils are in developing countries; in Africa yield reduction is 2–40%, an average loss of 8.2% for the continent.
Eroded soil carries nitrogen, phosphorus, farm chemicals and pollutants such as heavy metals into surface water, raising turbidity and risking eutrophication.
Degradation can disturb soil microbes, remove climax vegetation and shrink animal habitat, leading to biodiversity loss; floods degrade soil and degraded soil causes floods.
Degradation sharpens competition for farmland: all except 3 internal conflicts in African states in the 1990s are linked to such competition.
Land degradation is estimated to cost US$44 billion a year, while the annual loss of 76 billion tons of soil costs the world about US$400 billion a year.

notes: Merges Land degradation#Impacts with Soil retrogression and degradation#Consequences of soil regression and degradation, which cover the same effects. The two yearly cost figures (US$44 billion for land degradation, S:c1016683d23d; US$400 billion for 76 billion tons of soil, S:44a0cdab7922) measure different things, so they are not listed as conflicts.

definition.text: Two measures that together describe how vulnerable a landscape is to degradation.

facts.text: Sensitivity is the degree to which a land system changes under natural forces, human intervention or both.
Resilience is a landscape's ability to absorb change without altering the balance of species in its community, and to return to its original state afterwards.
Land-use management can raise or lower resilience; degraded land is less resilient, so shocks can drive it into further degradation.

definition.text: The degradation of agricultural land, shaped by farmers' local choices and by global drivers such as trade, climate change and demographic change.

facts.text: By 2025 unsustainable farming had degraded 996 Mha of agricultural land, over 60% of all human-induced land degradation.
In high-income countries, heavy fertilizer use masks severe per-hectare losses but brings diminishing returns and can worsen degradation through acidification, nutrient imbalances and pollution.
Sub-Saharan Africa shows low degradation-induced yield losses mainly because limited access to inputs, machinery, credit and markets dominates its yield gaps.
In 2025, 47 million stunted children under five lived where stunting overlaps significant yield losses from degradation; Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa combine degraded land with high poverty.

definition.text: Managing land in ways that prevent and reverse its degradation while conserving soil and water.

facts.text: Actions to halt land degradation fall broadly into prevention, mitigation and restoration.
It raises soil moisture and infiltration while cutting runoff, erosion and flood discharge, which supports water security.
Reversing just 10% of human-induced cropland degradation could feed an additional 154 million people a year; restoring abandoned cropland could feed between 292 and 476 million.
Because degradation also harms pastures and wider ecosystem services, restoring land requires collective action to provide these public goods.
Regenerative agriculture aims to reverse degradation through continuous ground cover, minimal soil disturbance, diverse crop rotations and rotational grazing.
Public awareness, education and outreach help people and communities adopt sustainable practices and act as stewards of the land.

title: Land degradation neutrality

definition.text: A policy goal, set in UN Sustainable Development Goal 15, of restoring degraded land and soil so that the world becomes land degradation-neutral by 2030.

facts.text: Target 15.3 reads: by 2030, combat desertification, restore degraded land and soil, including land hit by desertification, drought and floods, and strive for a land degradation-neutral world.
The Land Degradation Neutrality Fund, launched at UNCCD COP 13 in 2017, invests in projects with environmental, socio-economic and financial returns.
The Fund was initially capitalized at US$100 million and is expected to grow to US$300 million; the European Investment Bank agreed to invest up to $45 million.
Supporting land degradation neutrality is one objective of the UNCCD's 2018–2030 Strategic Framework.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
notes: No article of its own; mentioned on Land degradation and United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification. S:8e427fdb5c28 dates the EIB investment to 2009, but S:9213116a46d8 says the Fund launched in 2017: one date may be wrong, so the year is left out of the fact.

title: Desertification

definition.text: The gradual degradation of fertile land into arid desert through a combination of natural processes and human activities.

facts.text: Its immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation, driven alone or together by drought, climatic shifts, acid rain, tillage, overgrazing and deforestation for fuel or building materials.
In many environments the rate of erosion and runoff falls exponentially as vegetation cover increases.
Unprotected dry topsoil blows away or washes off in flash floods, leaving infertile lower layers that bake in the sun into an unproductive hardpan.
Some 10–20% of drylands are estimated to be degraded, 6 to 12 million square kilometres are affected, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification.
The most affected areas are the Sahel in Africa, the Gobi Desert and Mongolia in Asia, and parts of South America.
Its effects include sand and dust storms, food insecurity and poverty, and it is recognized as a major threat to biodiversity.
Remedies include improving soil quality, greening deserts, managing grazing, and reforestation and afforestation.
Wind erosion, especially when people raise it far above natural rates, is a major source of desertification, and erosion can end in desertification.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Definitions of desertification

definition.text: The competing formal definitions of desertification, of which more than 100 existed by 2005.

facts.text: The UNCCD defines it as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions resulting from factors including climatic variations and human activities.
That definition ties desertification to land use and land management and highlights its economic, social and environmental implications.
The original idea that desertification meant the physical expansion of deserts has been rejected as the concept evolved.
Sub-groupings such as 'man-made desert' and 'non-pattern desert' are also disputed.

related: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
contested_note: Sources report considerable controversy over the proper definition, with more than 100 formal definitions as of 2005, and dispute some sub-types.
distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Causes of desertification

definition.text: The natural and human factors that strip land of most of its vegetation and turn it into desert.

facts.text: Overgrazing lets livestock feed on land for long periods without replanting grass, leaving it bare to harden in the sun and lose nutrients to the wind.
Overcultivation and monocropping drain soil nutrients; depleted soil loses organic matter and its ability to hold moisture, then hardens and cracks.
Intensive farming to maximize yields needs more fertilizer, pesticides and machinery, and continuous use rapidly depletes soil nutrients.
Population growth turns once-acceptable practices into unsustainable overgrazing, over-farming and deforestation.
The Sahara owes its existence to natural changes in solar insolation from Earth's orbital precession, which alter the West African Monsoon and trigger vegetation and dust feedbacks.
Regional studies find soil health, human activities and weather all contribute, in different balances: in Shaanxi, meteorological factors work against desertification while the soil worsens it.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Human role in desertification

definition.text: The dispute over how far local human overexploitation, rather than natural climate variability, drives desertification.

facts.text: Early studies named overgrazing, the overconsumption of vegetation by livestock, as one of the most common causes of desertification.
Sahel drought is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall variability set by sea surface temperatures, which are driven by natural variability, sulphate aerosols and greenhouse gases.
Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions have re-greened the Sahel, leading some scholars to call agriculture-induced vegetation loss a minor factor.
Overgrazing by local cattle may have partly driven the mid-Holocene change of the Sahara from savanna to desert.
Studies of critical regions confirm that human activities and soil health join meteorological factors as main contributors to desertification.

contested_note: Sources call the role of local overexploitation in recent desertification controversial, and some scholars treat agriculture-induced vegetation loss as a minor factor.
distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Climate change and desertification

definition.text: The role of a warming climate in expanding the world's drylands and driving desertification.

facts.text: Drylands are expected to grow from 38% of the continents in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by the end of the century under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5.
Most of the expansion is expected in southwest North America, the northern fringe of Africa, southern Africa and Australia.
A 2020 attribution study found 6% of the world's drylands underwent desertification between 1982 and 2015, driven by unsustainable land use compounded by human-caused climate change.
Despite average global greening, human-caused climate change has degraded 12.6% (5.43 million km2) of drylands, affecting 213 million people, 93% of them in developing economies.
Research is complex because no single metric captures every aspect of desertification.

related: Effects of climate change on agriculture
distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Drylands

definition.text: Zones defined by scarce water, where precipitation is balanced by evaporation and plant evapotranspiration; UNEP counts tropical and temperate areas with an aridity index below 0.65.

facts.text: Drylands fall into four sub-types: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid lands; the UNCCD leaves hyper-arid zones out of its definition.
They cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface, including 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America, and are home to more than 2 billion people.
Drylands include 45% of the world's agricultural land and are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate and land-use change.
72% of drylands lie in developing countries, and almost all hyper-arid land does.
Unlike more humid biomes, drylands redistribute water mostly through above-ground runoff.
Arid lands make up about 10% of the world's land; hyper-arid lands cover about 8% and get irregular rain barely above 100 mm.
From 1982 to 2015, 12.6% of the world's drylands degraded because of human-caused climate change, and about 7.6% of global land has shifted to drier conditions.
Pressure to farm marginal drylands brings overgrazing, land exhaustion and overdrafting of groundwater to many poorer countries.

conflicts.text: Drylands covered 38% of the continents in the late 20th century.
conflicts.note: Drylands page gives 41.3% (S:af37f5772f34); may reflect a different baseline.

conflicts.text: 44% of agricultural land lies in drylands.
conflicts.note: S:fbe4f37dbc0c gives 45% of the world's agricultural land.

conflicts.text: Arid land (aridity index 0.05-0.20) covers 12.1% of global land.
conflicts.note: Drylands page says arid lands make up about 10% (S:05a0651b0914).

notes: Extended in gap-fill from the Drylands article.

title: Desertification and dust storms

definition.text: Storms of wind-blown sand and dust that become more frequent as desertification leaves more loose material for the wind to pick up.

facts.text: Global annual dust emissions rose 25% between the late nineteenth century and the present day.
Middle Eastern dust storms are becoming more frequent and intense as long-term rainfall decline lowers soil moisture and plant cover.
Dust storms contribute to respiratory disorders such as pneumonia and asthma, pollute open water and can halt most transport.
Airborne dust scatters sunlight and warms the atmosphere, shortening cloud lifetimes and reducing rainfall, which can worsen desertification.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Desertification and food insecurity

definition.text: The threat desertification poses to global food security by shrinking the land that can be farmed sustainably.

facts.text: 44% of agricultural land is in drylands, and it supplies 60% of the world's food production.
Food demand keeps growing with population while desertification removes sustainable farmland, so demand may soon exceed supply.
Climate change, land degradation and population growth have worsened violent herder–farmer conflicts in Nigeria, Sudan, Mali and other Sahel countries.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Desertification and poverty

definition.text: The deepening poverty of dryland communities as desertification lowers land productivity and pushes people off the land.

facts.text: Investors avoid low-potential arid zones, and without infrastructure, markets and suitable techniques most such zones are excluded from development.
When rural land can no longer support its population, people migrate to cities, particularly in Africa, creating unemployment and slums.
Environmental refugees in sub-Saharan Africa are projected to rise from 14 million in 2010 to nearly 200 million by 2050.
In Mongolia, where the land is 90% fragile dryland, many herders migrate to the city for work.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Desertification in the Sahel

definition.text: Desertification in Africa's Sahel, a hot dry belt with 100–600 mm of rain a year, where climate change and human activity combine.

facts.text: The Sahel has lost approximately 650,000 km2 of productive agricultural land over the past 50 years.
The Sahara has swung between wet grassland and dry desert every 20,000 years, linked to a roughly 40,000-year cycle in Earth's axial tilt between 22° and 24.5°.
Since 1900 the Sahara has reportedly expanded 250 km southward along a 6,000 km west–east front.
Lake Chad has shrunk by over 90% since 1987 through irrigation withdrawals and lower rainfall, displacing millions of people.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

definition.text: The spread of the Gobi Desert across northern China and southern Mongolia, the fastest-expanding desert on Earth.

facts.text: The Gobi turns over 3,600 km2 of grassland into wasteland each year, and large sand dunes are forming only 70 km from Beijing.
About 13% of Mongolia's desertification is put down to natural factors and the rest mainly to overgrazing and erosion of cultivated soils; over 70% of its land is degraded.
From 1940 to 2015 Mongolia's mean air temperature rose by 2.24 °C while precipitation fell by 7%, making conditions more arid.
A shift from sheep to goats to meet cashmere export demand has degraded grazing land, because goats eat roots and flowers.

title: Desertification in South America

definition.text: Desertification across South America, where 25% of the land is drylands and over 68% has suffered soil erosion from deforestation and overgrazing.

facts.text: Between 27 and 43% of the land in Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador and Peru is at risk of desertification.
In Argentina, Mexico and Paraguay more than half the land is degraded by desertification and cannot be farmed.
Rural Mexico loses about 1,000 km2 of land a year to desertification, and drought in Central America has driven unemployment, food insecurity and migration.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Reversing desertification

definition.text: Techniques and countermeasures that mitigate or reverse desertification.

facts.text: One barrier is that sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when they benefit society and the environment.
Lack of political will and of funding for land reclamation and anti-desertification programmes also holds progress back.
Some countries have biodiversity action plans to protect endangered flora and fauna from desertification.
The FAO launched its Drylands Restoration Initiative in 2012 and in 2015 published global guidelines for restoring degraded dryland forests and landscapes.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 15 adds global advocacy for combating desertification and restoring affected land.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Soil improvement against desertification

definition.text: Techniques that supply water to dryland soils and fix and enrich them to halt desertification.

facts.text: Shelter belts, woodlots and windbreaks of trees and bushes fix the soil, reducing erosion and evapotranspiration; sand fences control drifting sand.
Short of water, clay soils can consolidate instead of staying porous; techniques such as zaï or tillage then still allow crops to be planted.
Contour trenching digs 150 m long, 1 m deep trenches along the contour, edged with stone walls, so water cannot flow and cause erosion.
Plants restore fertility, chiefly nitrogen-fixing legumes, succulents such as Opuntia, and food crops and trees such as grains, barley, beans and dates.
Nitrogen-rich fertilizer also restores fertility, but its cost deters smallholders, so India, Zambia and Malawi subsidize it.
Research centres are inoculating arid-zone trees with mycorrhizal fungi, which greatly enlarge the root surface that gathers nutrients.
Bioengineering soil microbes, especially photosynthesizers, has been modelled as a way to strengthen the cooperative loops between microbes and vegetation in drylands.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Desert greening

definition.text: Reclaiming deserts and desertified land, with methods matched to each kind of desert.

facts.text: Salt flats in Saudi Arabia's Rub' al Khali are among the most promising sites for seawater agriculture, which needs no freshwater and little energy.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration has reclaimed some 30,000 square kilometers of degraded land in Niger.
Ethiopia's Humbo Assisted Regeneration Project uses these techniques with money from the World Bank's BioCarbon Fund, which backs carbon sequestration in forests and farmland.
Large tree-planting belts are the best-known approach: China's Green Wall and the African Union's Great Green Wall along the Sahara.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Farmer-managed natural regeneration

definition.text: A low-cost land restoration technique in which farmers regrow and manage trees and shrubs from living stumps, roots and seeds.

facts.text: Australian agricultural economist Tony Rinaudo developed it in West Africa in the 1980s, adapting the centuries-old practices of coppicing and pollarding.
Seemingly bare fields hold an 'underground forest' of living stumps; each can send up 10 to 30 stems, of which the tallest and straightest are kept.
Trees kept among crops and pastures raise yields, soil fertility, organic matter and soil moisture, and reduce wind damage and soil erosion.
Pruned residue mulches fields, raising soil water retention and cutting evaporation.
Trials and long-running programs suggest it can at least double crop yields on low-fertility soils.
Faidherbia albida, the 'fertiliser tree', fixes nitrogen, and its leaf fall adds nutrients and organic matter to the soil.
By 2004 it was practised on over five million hectares, half of Niger's farmland, after nurseries and tree planting had largely failed.
From the 1930s until 1993, Niger's forestry laws took tree ownership out of people's hands, a major obstacle later eased by property-law changes.

conflicts.text: The method has enabled farmers to regenerate some 30,000 square kilometers in Niger.
conflicts.note: FMNR page gives over five million hectares (50,000 km2) by 2004 (S:7755ee15e2f4).

notes: Extended in gap-fill from its own article.

title: Three-North Shelter Forest Program

definition.text: China's Great Green Wall: planted windbreak forest strips (shelterbelts), begun in 1978, meant to hold back the Gobi Desert and supply timber.

facts.text: It is planned to finish around 2050 as a barrier about 4,828 km long and up to 1,448 km wide, covering around 88 million acres of forest.
It set out to raise northern China's forest cover from 5 to 15 percent; 29.7% of China had been desertified by 2000, driven by water use, mining, excess farming and wood cutting.
The Gobi grew by 10,000 square kilometres a year in the 1980s but was shrinking by more than 2,000 square kilometres a year in 2022.
By 2009 China's planted forest covered more than 500,000 square kilometres, the largest artificial forest in the world.
In 2024 China finished a 3,000 km green belt around the Taklamakan Desert; desert cover fell from 27.2% to 26.8% over a decade.
Reforestation raised evapotranspiration more than rainfall, and the forests dry the soil more than farmland; dense exotic plantings on the Loess Plateau may worsen water shortages.
A 2023 study found only a fifth of surviving forests became forest stands within 10 years and a tenth were alive after 40.
Monoculture planting left trees open to disease: in 2000 one billion poplars in Ningxia were lost to a single disease.

related: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia
contested_note: Reports credit it with reversing the Gobi's spread, while critics question tree survival, water use and whether it addresses the causes of desertification.

conflicts.text: Proposed in the late 1970s, the project is not predicted to end until 2055.
Desert land has shrunk by an annual average of 1,980 square km.
conflicts.note: The article gives more than 2,000 km2 a year in 2022 (S:15cb9069db7b); different periods.

notes: Also called the Great Green Wall (China); extended in gap-fill from that article.

title: Great Green Wall (Africa)

definition.text: An African Union project adopted in 2007, first conceived as a belt of trees across the Sahel from Djibouti to Dakar to combat desertification and hold back the Sahara.

facts.text: The wall was to be 15 km wide and 7,775 km long, but it grew into a mosaic of water harvesting, protected greenery and improved indigenous land use.
Its goal is to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs by 2030.
It aims to help the ground retain seasonal rainfall, supporting land rehabilitation and future farming.
In the 1950s Richard St. Barbe Baker proposed a 'Green front', a 50-kilometre-deep tree buffer against the expanding desert.
A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered; about 18 million hectares were restored by 2023 and about 30 million by 2024.
Nigeria has restored 4.9 million hectares of degraded land and Ethiopia has reclaimed 15 million hectares.
Critics point to the colonial origins of the term 'desertification', mostly European funding, and top-down strategies that push sedentarization.
Little monitoring has been done, and by 2023 the project faced a risk of collapse from terrorist threats, lack of political leadership and too little funding.

contested_note: Progress figures differ widely, and critics question the project's colonial framing, funding and top-down design.

conflicts.text: The project combats desertification in 20 countries.

conflicts.note: The article gives 7,775 km long and 15 km wide (S:b84586aca331); 'wide' here probably means long.

conflicts.text: The project has restored 36 million hectares of land.
conflicts.note: The article gives about 30 million hectares as of 2024 (S:027ae82e42f2).

conflicts.text: As of 2022, over 56 000 ha of degraded lands have been restored.
conflicts.note: Far below the 18 million ha for 2023 (S:b1cf864b62a2); may count a narrower set of projects.

title: Managed grazing

definition.text: Grazing that moves herds through many small fenced paddocks every day or two, mimicking natural grazers so the grass can regrow.

facts.text: Restored grasslands store atmospheric CO2 as plant material, whereas confined grazing livestock keep grass growth low.
Proponents claim wider use could raise soil carbon across the world's 3.5 billion hectares of agricultural grassland and offset nearly 12 years of CO2 emissions.
Many researchers dispute these claims, saying it neither reverses desertification nor offsets its emissions.

contested_note: Proponents claim large soil-carbon gains, but many researchers say it neither reverses desertification nor offsets emissions.
distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Agrivoltaics in deserts

definition.text: Pairing solar panels with planted vegetation in deserts to support ecosystem function even where rain is scarce.

facts.text: A 2025 study in the Kubuqi Desert, which gets around 300 mm of rain a year, found microbial counts, soil quality and nutrients improved most under integrated agrivoltaic systems.
Panel shade cut soil temperature and evaporation, the panels acted as windbreaks that stopped sand burying plants, and with the vegetation they created a better microclimate.
A 2 GW project in Inner Mongolia plans to apply this at scale to restore vegetation, stabilize dunes and weaken dust storms.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: History of desertification

definition.text: The long natural history of deserts, which grew and shrank mostly independently of people, and the later study of human-driven land deterioration.

facts.text: Paleodeserts are large sand seas now stabilized by vegetation, some reaching beyond the present margins of core deserts such as the Sahara.
Centuries ago, severe land deterioration in arid regions centred on three densely populated areas: the Mediterranean, the Mesopotamian Valley and China's Loess Plateau.
The earliest known discussion followed the French colonization of West Africa, when the Comité d'Etudes commissioned a study of the prehistoric spread of the Sahara.
The modern study of desertification emerged from research on the 1980s drought in the Sahel.

distinct_from: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia

title: Soil sealing

definition.text: The loss of soil resources when land is covered over for housing, roads or other construction.

facts.text: Topsoil is covered or replaced by asphalt and cement and the layers below are compacted, a mostly irreversible loss of soil ecosystem services.
Sealed land is a serious form of land take; together they cause complete loss of the soil's biological, physical and chemical functions.
Sealed surfaces hinder infiltration and increase surface runoff, and sealing for underground construction alters water movement and weakens the soil's ability to purify water.
Heat-absorbing concrete and asphalt without cooling vegetation create urban heat islands.
Fertile farmland converted to buildings no longer produces food; countries with fast-growing populations and economies are losing notable areas of farmland this way.
Sealing fragments habitats and causes soil biodiversity loss, worsened by falling soil carbon, nitrogen and respiration.
It removes urban green spaces that offer cultural benefits such as recreation, learning and a sense of belonging.
Sealing is assessed with raindrop impact tests in the field and laboratory and with indices such as the NDVI and the Normalized Difference Built-up Index.

notes: Sealing here means covering soil with built surfaces; the surface sealing by crusting mentioned on Surface irrigation and Base-cation saturation ratio belongs with Soil crust.

definition.text: Removing asphalt, cement and other human-made covers so that a sealed soil can again perform its natural functions.

facts.text: Because sealing losses are mostly irreversible, unsealing is very difficult, and research on it is very limited.
Urban, barren or old dumping soils can become parks, green roofs and gardens, but only after thorough decontamination.
Under the 'no net land take' principle used in the Walloon Region and Germany, sealed surfaces are removed to offset new urban projects.
A Palermo field trial found vegetated de-sealing stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity over eighteen months, while crushed asphalt kept higher permeability but less plant cover.

title: Grassland degradation

definition.text: A biotic disturbance, also called vegetation or steppe degradation, in which grass struggles to grow or disappears from land through overgrazing, burrowing small mammals or climate change.

facts.text: Since the 1970s it has affected alpine meadows and grasslands, notably in the Philippines and in China's Tibetan and Inner Mongolian region, where 2,460 km2 is degraded each year.
It takes years or decades: dead brown patches appear first and, if untreated, spread over many acres, and restoration is just as slow.
Warming speeds evaporation and both heavy rain and drought hinder grass, but some scientists dismiss climate change as an insignificant cause.
Roads, herders' settlements with their animals, monocropping of converted grassland, deforestation and medicinal plant gathering also degrade grassland.
Less arable land and lower harvests push farmers onto smaller plots that are more easily overgrazed and exhausted, and livestock numbers fall.
On the Tibetan Plateau 15–20% of species are now endangered, and carbon and nitrogen losses cost $8,033/ha and $13,315/ha respectively.
With fewer plants to anchor the soil, erosion and dust storms increase, and more carbon and nitrogen may escape to the atmosphere.
In northern China, grassland degradation affects 400 million people a year, with 54 billion yuan of annual economic loss.

related: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia
contested_note: Most sources link grassland degradation to climate change, but some scientists dismiss it as an insignificant cause.
notes: The lead's global figure of 23% of land degraded (S:46641a99cd1c) is another share-of-land estimate; see Global extent of land degradation.

title: Overgrazing

definition.text: Grazing in which animals eat grass faster than it can grow back, as when pastures are stocked above the livestock carrying capacity.

facts.text: It is thought to be the principal cause of grassland degradation and is a farming activity that causes desertification.
Urbanization leaves less farmland, so farmers pack small plots densely with animals and must gather much grass for long alpine winters.
Rapid eating and constant trampling stop grass regrowing, and the suppressed sward invites rats and insects that further inhibit growth.
It is a main cause of shrub and bush encroachment in grasslands and savannas.
Overgrazing is among the improper farming practices that accelerate soil erosion and degrade land.
Continued overuse leaves soils so poor that only drought-tolerant and early successional plants can grow.
A meta-analysis of 148 studies found most ecosystem functions decline as grazing intensity rises, and aridity weakens the benefits of light grazing.
Hardin's 1968 Tragedy of the Commons used overgrazing as its example, though English common land was historically protected by stinting, a cap on each commoner's animals.

notes: Section entry; overgrazing recurs on Land degradation, Desertification, Soil retrogression and degradation and Agricultural pollution.

title: Small mammals in grassland degradation

definition.text: Damage to grassland blamed on growing populations of burrowing small mammals such as marmots, voles, pikas and zokors.

facts.text: Burrowing and gnawing encourage soil erosion and make it hard for plants to root, leaving grass patchy.
Others argue that burrowing recycles soil nutrients and that the population rise simply follows increased grazing.
Rodent control, by shooting, sterilizing or low-toxicity poison such as Botulin toxin C, aims to manage populations rather than wipe them out.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether burrowing mammals cause grassland degradation or merely follow heavier grazing.

definition.text: The three sequential stages of grassland degradation: light, moderate and high.

facts.text: Lightly degraded grassland has patches of dead or missing grass scattered across the land.
In moderately degraded grassland, dead patches grow in size and number, plant and animal diversity clearly falls, and pests such as rats and insects damage soil and plants.
Highly degraded grassland is a vast expanse of dead grass, neither arable nor fit for livestock, with very low diversity and a few poisonous plants.
Severely degraded grassland is called heitutan, or black beach or black-soil-land: bare, unusable black soil extending 10–15 cm below ground level.

definition.text: Restoring degraded grassland with methods matched to how severely it is degraded.

facts.text: Success needs recognition in policy, standard indicators of degradation, scientific innovation, knowledge transfer and data sharing, and early action makes it easier.
Lightly degraded land can be fenced from grazing, fertilized or weeded; grazing may continue at lower, monitored intensity, for example by rotating fields seasonally.
Moderately degraded land needs reseeding and rodent control; active brush control can restore areas invaded by woody plants.
Highly degraded land with 30% or more plant cover gets semi-artificial grassland; worse heitutan land needs artificial grassland with weed and rodent control, plowing, seeding and fertilizing.

title: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
article: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

definition.text: An international convention (UNCCD) to combat desertification and ease the effects of drought through national action programmes backed by international cooperation.

facts.text: The only convention stemming directly from the Rio Conference's Agenda 21, it was adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994 and entered into force in December 1996.
It is the only internationally legally binding framework on desertification, built on participation, partnership and decentralization.
It has 197 parties, including all 193 UN member states and the European Union; Canada withdrew in 2013 and rejoined in 2017.
The Conference of the Parties, of all ratifying governments, is its supreme decision-making body; its sessions were annual from 1997 to 2001 and are biennial since.
A Committee on Science and Technology, with a Group of Experts, sets research priorities and reviews data on the natural and human causes of desertification.
National Action Programmes, developed with local communities, set out the practical steps against desertification in specific ecosystems and are its key instruments.
Its 2018–2030 Strategic Framework, adopted in 2017, aims to restore affected ecosystems, support land degradation neutrality, improve living conditions and strengthen drought resilience.
At COP16 in Riyadh in December 2024, more than US$12 billion was pledged against desertification, land degradation and drought.

contested_note: Sources report debate over how effective the 2006 International Year of Deserts and Desertification, declared to publicise the Convention, was in practice.
notes: Summary entry for the convention; its secretariat (Bonn since January 1999, S:52c6a8fb2195), COP list and Group of Experts are folded in. The contested point is S:0c1158605422.

title: Land consumption

definition.text: The conversion of land with healthy soil and intact habitats into industrial farmland, roads and especially urban settlements.

facts.text: The European Environment Agency names three land-consuming activities: expansion of built-up area, the extent of land exploited for farming, forestry and other uses, and over-intensive exploitation of farm and forest land.
Because these activities are virtually irreversible, the term land loss is also used; erosion and desertification also cause land loss, mostly traceable to people.
From 1990 to 2000 the U.S. consumed 1.4 million hectares of open space, and Germany consumes more than 70 hectares every day.
Land take in 21 EU countries is estimated at about 1.2 million hectares over 1990–2006.
A region's land footprint, the area needed at home and abroad for what it consumes, can far exceed its own land; Europe depends most on such imported land.
Its effects include habitat loss, loss or contamination of topsoil, compaction that eradicates soil life, and impervious surfaces that disrupt water and biogeochemical cycles.
The land economy still lacks environmental full-cost accounting for the long-term costs of environmental degradation.

notes: The page also gives a second sense, forced displacement of people from their land by land grabbing (S:a3df7fa9fced), which is left out.

definition.text: Work to return degraded drylands to their former function, or to manage them so they degrade no further.

facts.text: It is especially hard because rain is rare and variable, temperatures are high, soils are infertile and invasive species spread.
Restoration islands are small, well-placed plantings that spread into neighbouring ground, suiting patchy dryland vegetation and reducing soil erosion.
Soil fauna improve soil structure, nutrient cycling and infiltration; they can be helped with endemic species, nucleation sites and mulching to keep the soil moist.
Rangelands cover about 25% of drylands, and their restoration counts as a climate mitigation option because of its carbon sequestration potential.

definition.text: A numerical indicator of how dry the climate is at a given place.

facts.text: Aridity is permanent, whereas drought is temporary.
UNEP's 1992 index compares average annual precipitation with potential evapotranspiration in the same units, so it rises as conditions get wetter.
Its classes are hyperarid (below 0.05, 7.5% of land), arid (0.05-0.20, 12.1%), semi-arid (0.20-0.50, 17.7%) and dry subhumid (0.50-0.65, 9.9%).
One of the first indices, by Köppen and Geiger, set an annual rainfall threshold that depends on mean annual temperature and the season the rain falls in.

title: Woody plant encroachment

definition.text: The spread and thickening of native woody plants, bushes and shrubs at the expense of grasses and forbs.

facts.text: Encroachers are native to the ecosystem, unlike introduced invasive species; they count as encroachers when they outcompete other native species.
It occurs mainly in grasslands, savannas and woodlands on all continents, about 500 million hectares, and can turn open grassland into closed woodland.
Rates reach 1 percent per decade in the Eurasian steppes, 10-20 percent in North America, 8 percent in South America, 2.4 percent in Africa and 1 percent in Australia.
It has occurred at unparalleled rates since the mid-19th century and is classed as a type of grassland degradation.
It is often treated as land degradation that harms biodiversity, groundwater recharge, carbon storage and grazing capacity, but some argue it is natural succession.
In arid lands it has been called 'green desertification', though grass between the canopies can survive, whereas desertification leaves bare soil without organic matter.
Soil quality declines under encroachment in arid and semi-arid regions but often improves in Mediterranean and very humid climates, with more topsoil carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus.
In North America, each 1 percent increase in woody cover cuts carrying capacity by 0.6 to 1.6 cattle per 100 hectares.

contested_note: Sources treat it both as a symptom of land degradation and as a form of natural succession, with context-dependent impacts.

title: Causes of woody plant encroachment

definition.text: Local land-use drivers such as overgrazing, fire suppression and the loss of wild herbivores, together with global drivers such as rising CO2, that favour woody plants over grasses.

facts.text: By the two-layer theory, grasses use topsoil moisture and woody plants subsoil moisture, so overgrazing grass lets more water reach the subsoil for woody plants.
Coarse-textured soils promote woody growth while fine-textured soils limit it, and moisture and nutrients make downslope and cooler slopes more prone.
Woody plants with the C3 photosynthetic pathway thrive under high CO2, unlike C4 grasses.
When rainfall intensity rises, deep soil water usually increases, which benefits bushes more than grasses.

related: Effects of climate change on agriculture

definition.text: The change in ecosystem carbon when woody plants invade grassland: a sink if only above-ground biomass is counted, but uncertain once grass and soil organic carbon losses are included.

facts.text: Several studies find above-ground carbon gains entirely offset by below-ground losses.
Soil organic carbon tends to rise under encroachment in dry ecosystems and fall in mesic ones; in tropical savanna soils most of it comes from grass.
A meta-analysis of 142 studies found changes in soil organic carbon (0-50 cm) from -50 to 300 percent, with gains under leguminous shrubs and on sandy soils.
Rooting depth increases with encroachment, on average by 38 cm and up to 65 cm.

title: Woody encroachment and soil water
article: Woody plant encroachment#Groundwater recharge and soil moisture

definition.text: The link between woody encroachment and reduced groundwater recharge, because bushes use far more rainwater than grasses and alter streamflow.

facts.text: Denser canopies raise transpiration and evaporation of soil moisture, and enhanced soil porosity can speed soil drought.
In South Africa about 44% of rainfall is caught by woody canopies and evaporated, and up to 10% less rain enters the soil.
In arid and semi-arid lands encroachment reduces stream flows, while woody plant control can improve the connectivity of water resources.

definition.text: Action to manage the density and composition of bushes and shrubs in an area, also called brush management.

facts.text: Encroaching native woody plants are to be thinned, not eradicated, because they still provide functions such as animal habitat.
Measures are preventive (suitable stocking rates and rotational grazing), responsive (bush thinning) or maintenance (keeping the thinned density).
Prevention is thought cheaper than treatment, and control works best early in encroachment, at around 3% shrub cover.
Encroached grassland can be a stable state that will not recover without intervention, and chemical control can lose more carbon than mechanical thinning.

title: Deforestation

definition.text: The clearing of a forest or stand of trees and conversion of the land to non-forest uses such as farms, ranches or towns.

facts.text: Forests now cover about 31% of Earth's land, one-third less than before agriculture spread, with half that loss in the last century.
Agriculture is by far the main direct cause: in 2025 nearly 90% of global deforestation came from cropland expansion and pasture creation.
Topsoil often erodes once forests are cleared, raising sediment in rivers; tree roots bind soil, so cleared slopes become more prone to landslides.
Clearing alters soil microbial communities and reduces soil properties such as hydraulic conductivity, with sandier soils hit harder than clayey ones.
In an Amazon simulation, surface and soil temperatures rose by 1 to 3 °C after clearing, and changed soil properties could turn the soil into a carbon source.
Repeated slash-and-burn with shortened fallows leaves less vegetation and lower soil biomass on burned land.

related: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

definition.text: The giving up of farmed land, after which, for example, woody plants may re-establish on it.

facts.text: Threshold effects of land degradation may lead to abandonment in areas with a long history of intensive farming.
Abandonment can lead to woody plant encroachment as trees and shrubs re-establish on former farmland.
Farmland values in parts of southern Europe are projected to fall by more than 80% by 2100 under climate change, which could cause abandonment.

definition.text: The science and practice of conserving and sustainably managing rangelands, manipulating their components to yield the best mix of goods and services over time.

facts.text: It developed in the United States in response to rangeland deterioration from overgrazing and misuse of arid lands, shown by the Dust Bowl.
Historically it focused on managing grazing and the proper use of range vegetation for livestock.
Today it seeks to protect and enhance soils, riparian zones, watersheds and vegetation while sustaining products such as meat, water, wood and fibre.
Its scope has widened to the ecosystem services rangelands provide, and growing degradation, such as woody plant encroachment, makes rehabilitation part of the work.
Rangelands are highly vulnerable to climate change: heatwaves, droughts and floods are expected to alter ecological states and cut forage production.
Range science draws on animal science, plant ecology, soil science, wildlife management, climatology and anthropology.
